technical.title: Technical background — bathtub waste-and-overflow trip lever

cells: The trip lever operates a hidden linkage behind the tub wall connected to the stopper; diagnosis starts by removing the overflow cover plate and inspecting the links
Explains why a seized linkage is not visible from the tub side
Drain shoe, linkage assembly, overflow plate and trap form the system; the overflow plate is a safety feature
Defines the concealed assembly at issue
Remove the two screws in the overflow plate and pull the plate away; the upper linkage should follow
Supports the preferred from-above approach when the linkage is free
For stubborn drains, access the plumbing from below the tub; extreme cases may require cutting out old drain components from below
Explains why five-plus plumbers recommended below access
Installing a new kit requires aligning the rubber gasket and drain elbow from below while a helper holds the shoe from above
Concealed work usually needs an opening or access panel
Oatey publishes a full 'Dearborn Plastic Tubular Trip-Lever Bath Waste' kit with a chrome-finish stopper
Confirms the component type is a standard manufactured assembly
The overflow directs excess water into a concealed channel connected to the drain; traditional and integral types exist
Distinguishes the overflow plate from the trip-lever linkage
Trade guidance describes a hydrostatic / fill-and-inspect test of the drain and overflow connections
Plan access to the space below for a water test

technical.caption: All technical statements are linked to the publisher or manufacturer page they were read from on 2026-11-07. These sources describe typical assemblies and procedures; none of them inspected this specific bathtub, and none is San Francisco code guidance.
